name: Physics: Mechanics
author: Recurse
subject: science
description: Units, motion graphs, equations of motion, Newton's laws, forces, momentum and energy, with the classic misconceptions cleared up.

lesson.intro: Mechanics is the part of physics that explains how things move and why. A few ideas cover almost everything, from a dropped phone to a car crash: velocity and acceleration, Newton's three laws, momentum and energy. Several of them clash with everyday intuition, so this lesson points out the common traps as it goes.
objectives: Distinguish speed from velocity, and read slopes and areas on motion graphs
Solve constant-acceleration and free-fall problems with the equations of motion
Apply Newton's three laws with free-body diagrams that include weight, normal force and friction
Use conservation of momentum and impulse to analyze collisions and crashes
Calculate work, kinetic and potential energy and power, and apply conservation of energy

sections.title: Units, speed, velocity and acceleration
sections.body:
Physics uses the SI system so that everyone's numbers fit together. Three base units cover mechanics: the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass and the second (s) for time. Other units are built from them: a newton (N) is 1 kg·m/s², a joule (J) is 1 N·m, and a watt (W) is 1 J/s. Checking that the units on both sides of an equation match is a quick way to catch mistakes.

Speed and velocity are not the same thing:

- Distance is the total length of the path traveled. Displacement is the straight-line change in position, and it has a direction.
- Speed = distance / time. It has no direction.
- Velocity = displacement / time. It has a size and a direction, so it is a vector.
- Acceleration = change in velocity / time, measured in m/s². It is also a vector.

Because velocity includes direction, an object can accelerate without speeding up. A car going around a bend at a steady 50 km/h is accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. Slowing down is acceleration too, in the direction opposite to the motion.
sections.code:
speed        = distance / time
velocity     = displacement / time   (has a direction)
acceleration = change in velocity / time

Example: a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s
a = (20 m/s − 0 m/s) / 5 s = 4 m/s²
sections.tip: Ask whether direction matters. If it does, you need velocity, not speed.
sections.pitfall: Using speed and velocity interchangeably. A round trip can have a large average speed and an average velocity of zero.

check.question: A runner completes one 400 m lap in 80 s and finishes exactly where she started. What is her average velocity?
choices: 5 m/s
0 m/s
check.explanation: Her displacement is zero because she ends where she began, so her average velocity is zero. 5 m/s is her average speed: 400 m of distance divided by 80 s.

sections.title: Motion graphs: slopes and areas
sections.body:
A dashcam records a car's position every second. Plot position against time and the picture tells the story of the whole trip, if you know how to read it.

On a **position-time graph**, the slope is the velocity. A straight sloping line means constant velocity, and a steeper line means faster. A flat line means the object is standing still, and a line sloping down means it is moving back toward the start. A curve means the velocity is changing, so the object is accelerating, and the slope of the tangent at any point gives the velocity at that instant.

On a **velocity-time graph**, the slope is the acceleration and the **area** between the line and the time axis is the displacement. A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration); a line rising at a steady slope means constant acceleration. If the line crosses the time axis, the object stops for an instant and then moves the other way, and area below the axis counts as displacement backward.

Worked example: a car starts at 4 m/s and speeds up steadily to 16 m/s over 6 s.

- Acceleration = slope = (16 − 4) / 6 = 2 m/s².
- Displacement = area under the line, a trapezoid: (4 + 16) / 2 × 6 = 60 m. That is the same as the average velocity, 10 m/s, times 6 s.

The two graphs are linked: velocity is the slope of the position graph, and position accumulates the area under the velocity graph. Calculus calls these the derivative and the integral.
sections.code:
t (s)      0    1    2    3    4    5    6
v (m/s)    4    6    8   10   12   14   16

slope = (16 − 4) / 6 = 2 m/s²          acceleration
area  = (4 + 16) / 2 × 6 = 60 m        displacement
sections.pitfall: Reading a position-time graph as a picture of the path. A line going up does not mean the object is climbing a hill; it means its distance from the start is growing.

activity.title: Velocity-time graphs
activity.prompt: Treat the line as a velocity-time graph: x is time in seconds and y is velocity in m/s. Set b = 1 and a = 0.5 for an object starting at 1 m/s and gaining 0.5 m/s every second. Set a = 0 for constant velocity, then make a negative to show braking, and notice where the line crosses the time axis: the object stops for an instant there. Finally, match the target and name its starting velocity and acceleration.

check.question: A car's velocity-time graph is a straight line from 0 m/s to 12 m/s over 4 s. How far does the car travel in that time?
choices: 3 m
check.explanation: Distance is the area under the line, a triangle: ½ × 4 s × 12 m/s = 24 m. 48 m forgets the ½ (it treats the car as going 12 m/s the whole time), and 3 m/s² is the slope, the acceleration, not a distance.

sections.title: Newton's three laws
sections.body:
Newton's laws connect forces to changes in motion. A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons. What matters is the net force: the combined effect of all the forces on an object, taking their directions into account.

First law (inertia): an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net force acts on it. Motion does not need a force to keep it going. A hockey puck slows down because of friction, not because it runs out of force; on perfectly smooth ice it would glide forever.

Second law: net force = mass × acceleration, F = m·a. One newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s². The same force gives a larger mass a smaller acceleration, which is why a full shopping cart is harder to get moving than an empty one.

Third law: forces come in pairs. If object A pushes on object B, then B pushes on A with a force of equal size in the opposite direction. Both forces in a pair are the same kind of force: if Earth pulls you by gravity, you pull Earth by gravity. The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out. A rocket pushes exhaust gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward.
sections.code:
net force = all forces added, with direction
F = m · a        so        a = F / m

Push 30 N right and friction 10 N left on a 4 kg box:
net force = 30 N − 10 N = 20 N right
a = 20 N / 4 kg = 5 m/s² right
sections.tip: Forces change motion. They are not needed to keep motion going.
sections.pitfall: Thinking a moving object needs a force to keep it moving. Constant velocity means zero net force; forces cause changes in motion, not motion itself.

check.question: Earth pulls a book downward with a force we call its weight. What is the Newton's third law partner of this force?
choices: The table pushing up on the book
The book pushing down on the table
The book pulling up on Earth
Air pressing down on the book
check.explanation: A third law pair involves the same two objects with the roles swapped: Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls Earth, both by gravity. The table's upward push also acts on the book, so it cannot be the partner. It balances the weight only because the book is not accelerating.

sections.title: Gravity, normal force and friction
sections.body:
Three forces show up in almost every everyday problem.

Gravity. Near Earth's surface, gravity pulls every object down with a force called its weight: W = m·g, where g ≈ 9.8 m/s². A 70 kg person weighs about 70 × 9.8 ≈ 690 N. Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms, and is the same everywhere. Weight is a force, measured in newtons, and depends on where you are: on the Moon, g is about 1.6 m/s², so you would weigh about one sixth as much.

Falling objects. Without air resistance, every object falls with the same acceleration, g, whatever its mass. A heavier object does feel a bigger pull, but it also has more inertia, and the two effects cancel: a = W / m = m·g / m = g. A feather falls slowly on Earth only because of air resistance. On the Moon, which has no air, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together, and they landed at the same moment. Gravity also never switches off mid-flight: at the top of a throw a ball is still for an instant, but its acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downward.

Normal force. A surface pushes back on anything pressing on it, at right angles to the surface. A book resting on a flat table feels an upward normal force equal to its weight, so the net force on it is zero.

Friction. Friction acts along a surface and opposes sliding. Static friction holds a still object in place and grows to match your push, up to a maximum. Once the object slides, kinetic friction takes over, and it is usually a little smaller than that maximum. That is why a heavy box is harder to start moving than to keep moving.

The reliable method for any force problem is a **free-body diagram**: draw the object on its own, add an arrow for every force acting on it (weight, normal force, friction, pushes and pulls), choose a positive direction, add the forces to get the net force, then apply F = m·a.

Example: a 60 kg person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator that accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Taking up as positive, the forces are the scale's normal force N up and the weight m·g down, so N − m·g = m·a. Then N = 60 × (9.8 + 2) = 708 N. The scale reads more than the usual 588 N while the elevator speeds up on its way up, which is the heavy feeling you notice.
sections.code:
Weight:    W = m · g     (g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth, 1.6 m/s² on the Moon)
Falling:   a = W / m = g (the same for every mass, ignoring air)

70 kg person on Earth:   W = 70 × 9.8 ≈ 690 N
Same person on the Moon: W = 70 × 1.6 ≈ 110 N, mass still 70 kg
sections.tip: Mass is measured in kilograms and weight in newtons. Bathroom scales show kilograms only because they assume Earth's g.
sections.pitfall: Confusing mass and weight. Mass in kilograms stays the same everywhere; weight in newtons depends on the local g.

check.question: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon?
choices: About 13 kg
About 480 kg
80 kg
0 kg
check.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter, and it does not change with location, so it stays 80 kg. What changes is her weight, which drops to about one sixth: roughly 130 N instead of about 780 N.

sections.title: Equations of motion and projectiles
sections.body:
When the acceleration is constant, as for a car braking hard or anything in free fall, three equations link five quantities: initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a, time t and displacement s. Each equation leaves one quantity out, so pick the one that skips the quantity you neither know nor need.

- v = u + a·t (no s)
- s = u·t + ½·a·t² (no v)
- v² = u² + 2·a·s (no t)

Worked example: a car at 20 m/s brakes at 5 m/s², so a = −5 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping? We know u = 20 and v = 0, and we do not need t, so use v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 400 − 10s, so s = 40 m. Double the speed to 40 m/s and 0 = 1,600 − 10s gives s = 160 m. Twice the speed means four times the braking distance, the same v² that appears in kinetic energy.

Free fall is the same math with a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward. A stone dropped from rest falls s = ½ × 9.8 × t²: about 4.9 m in the first second and 19.6 m after two seconds.

**Projectiles** add one powerful idea: horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Gravity acts only vertically, so, ignoring air resistance, a thrown ball's horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical velocity changes by 9.8 m/s every second. A bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height at the same moment hit level ground at the same time; the fired one simply lands much farther away. The path is a parabola, and over level ground the longest range comes from a 45° launch angle.
sections.code:
Ball thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s (up is positive, a = −9.8 m/s²)

t (s)         0      1      2      3      4
v (m/s)     19.6    9.8    0    −9.8  −19.6
height (m)    0    14.7   19.6   14.7    0

The velocity drops by 9.8 m/s every second, and the motion is symmetric about the top.
sections.pitfall: Mixing sign conventions. Choose a positive direction at the start and stick to it: if up is positive, then g is −9.8 m/s² and a falling ball has a negative velocity.

activity.title: A throw as a position-time graph
activity.prompt: Read the curve as height (y) against time (x). Set a = −1, b = 4 and c = 0: a ball launched upward at 4 m/s under a gentle gravity of 2 m/s² (the x² coefficient is half the acceleration). Drag the tangent point: its slope is the velocity, positive on the way up, exactly 0 at the top (x = 2) and negative on the way down. Turn on the slope graph to see the velocity fall along a straight line.

check.question: A stone is dropped from rest off a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, how far does it fall in the first 3 seconds? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
check.explanation: s = ½·g·t² = ½ × 9.8 × 3² = 4.9 × 9 = 44.1 m. 29.4 m is its speed after 3 s (in m/s), not the distance, and 88.2 m forgets the ½.

sections.title: Momentum and its conservation
sections.body:
Momentum measures how hard it is to stop a moving object. It is mass times velocity: p = m·v, measured in kg·m/s. Like velocity, it has a direction. A slow-moving truck can have more momentum than a fast bicycle because its mass is so much larger.

Conservation of momentum: when no outside net force acts on a group of objects, their total momentum stays the same. The objects can trade momentum by pushing on each other, but those inside forces come in equal and opposite third law pairs, so the total never changes.

- Collisions: a 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits a still 1 kg cart and they stick together. The total momentum before is 2 × 3 = 6 kg·m/s, so afterwards the 3 kg pair moves at 6 / 3 = 2 m/s.
- Recoil: before a cannon fires, the total momentum is zero. Afterwards, the ball's forward momentum is matched by the cannon's equal backward momentum.

Changing an object's momentum takes force and time: force × time = change in momentum. This product is called impulse. An airbag or a car's crumple zone does not change how much momentum you lose in a crash, but it makes the stop take longer, so the force on you is smaller.

Momentum is conserved in every collision with no outside force, but kinetic energy usually is not: some of it turns into heat, sound and bent metal. Only in a perfectly elastic collision is kinetic energy conserved as well.
sections.code:
p = m · v
impulse = F · t = change in momentum

total momentum before = total momentum after
(2 kg)(3 m/s) + (1 kg)(0 m/s) = (3 kg)(v)
v = 2 m/s
sections.tip: For collision problems, write total momentum before = total momentum after, and use + and − signs for the two directions.
sections.pitfall: Expecting kinetic energy to be conserved in every collision. Momentum is conserved whenever no outside force acts, but kinetic energy only in perfectly elastic collisions.

check.question: A 60 kg skater and a 40 kg skater stand still on ice and push each other apart. The 40 kg skater moves off at 3 m/s. How fast does the 60 kg skater move?
choices: 3 m/s in the opposite direction
4.5 m/s in the opposite direction
0 m/s, because she did the pushing
2 m/s in the opposite direction
check.explanation: The total momentum starts at zero, so afterwards the two momenta must be equal and opposite. The 40 kg skater has 40 × 3 = 120 kg·m/s, so the 60 kg skater needs 120 / 60 = 2 m/s the other way. Both skaters move no matter who pushed, because the forces are a third law pair.

sections.title: Work, energy and power
sections.body:
Energy is the ability to cause change, measured in joules. You transfer energy to an object by doing work on it.

Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force: W = F·d. Pushing a box 3 m with a 50 N force does 150 J of work. If the object does not move, or moves at right angles to the force, that force does no work. Holding a heavy bag still is tiring, but you do no work on the bag.

Two forms of mechanical energy matter most:

- Kinetic energy, the energy of motion: KE = ½·m·v². Speed is squared, so doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large. This is why braking distance grows so quickly with speed.
- Gravitational potential energy, stored by height: PE = m·g·h. Lifting a 2 kg book 1.5 m stores 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 ≈ 29 J.

Conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred or changed from one form to another. A falling ball turns potential energy into kinetic energy. Friction and air resistance do not destroy energy; they turn some of it into heat and sound, which is why a bouncing ball never quite returns to its starting height.

Power is how fast energy is transferred: power = work / time, measured in watts, where 1 W = 1 J/s. Two people of the same weight climbing the same stairs do the same work, but the one who climbs faster has the higher power output.
sections.code:
W  = F · d         (joules)
KE = ½ · m · v²    (joules)
PE = m · g · h     (joules)
P  = W / t         (watts = joules per second)

Drop from 5 m, ignoring air resistance:
m·g·h = ½·m·v²   →   v = √(2·g·h) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5) ≈ 9.9 m/s
sections.tip: When a problem gives heights and speeds but no times, try conservation of energy before reaching for F = m·a.
sections.pitfall: Assuming every force does work. Holding a bag still, carrying a tray level, or pushing on a wall that does not move does no work on the object.

check.question: A ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Ignoring air resistance, what is true just before it hits the ground?
choices: All of its starting potential energy has become kinetic energy
Its total energy is greater than when it was dropped
It has used up all of its energy
Its kinetic energy is half of its starting potential energy
check.explanation: With no air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved: the potential energy lost on the way down equals the kinetic energy gained. The total stays the same, so it neither grows nor gets used up.

keyTerms.definition: Displacement per unit time: speed with a direction, so it is a vector.
The rate of change of velocity, in m/s². Speeding up, slowing down and turning all count.
The combined effect of all the forces on an object, taking direction into account.
An object's resistance to changes in its motion. More mass means more inertia.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m·g, measured in newtons. Not the same as mass.
Mass times velocity, p = m·v. Conserved when no outside net force acts.
The energy of motion, KE = ½·m·v².
The rate of doing work or transferring energy, in watts (joules per second).
The straight-line change in position, with a direction; the area under a velocity-time graph.
Force multiplied by the time it acts, equal to the change in momentum.
An object moving under gravity alone after launch; its horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical velocity changes by g each second.

summary: Velocity and acceleration have direction, so turning at a steady speed is still acceleration.
On a velocity-time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area is the displacement; with constant acceleration, v = u + at and v² = u² + 2as do the rest.
A net force changes motion (F = m·a); no force is needed to keep an object moving, and third law pairs act on different objects.
Without air resistance everything falls with g ≈ 9.8 m/s², and a projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
Momentum is conserved when no outside force acts, and impulse (force × time) explains why airbags help.
Energy is always conserved, though friction turns some into heat; kinetic energy grows with the square of the speed.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why a bowling ball and a tennis ball dropped together from a balcony land at almost the same time, and why a crash with an airbag hurts less than one without, using Newton's laws and momentum.

questions.question: Which combination of SI base units is equal to one newton?
choices: kg·m/s
kg·m/s²
kg·m²/s²
g·cm/s²
questions.explanation: From F = m·a, a newton is a kilogram times an acceleration in m/s², so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². kg·m/s is the unit of momentum, and kg·m²/s² is the joule, the unit of energy.

questions.question: A cyclist speeds up from 2 m/s to 14 m/s in 4 s. What is her average acceleration, in m/s²?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time: (14 − 2) / 4 = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s². A common slip is dividing the final speed by the time (14 / 4 = 3.5), which ignores the speed she started with.
questions.concept: acceleration from a change in velocity

questions.question: A car drives around a circular track at a steady 60 km/h. Is it accelerating?
choices: No, because its speed never changes
Only when it speeds up or brakes
Yes, because its direction is always changing
No, because it keeps returning to the same point
questions.explanation: Acceleration is any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. On a circle the direction changes every moment, so the car accelerates toward the center even at a constant speed. A steady speed only means the size of the velocity is fixed.

questions.question: A hockey puck glides across perfectly frictionless ice at a constant 5 m/s. What is the net force on it?
choices: Zero
A forward force that slowly runs out
A forward force proportional to its speed
A backward force equal to its weight
questions.explanation: By Newton's first law, an object moving at constant velocity has zero net force on it. Its weight is balanced by the ice's upward normal force, and nothing needs to push it forward. The idea that motion needs a force to keep going is the most common misconception in mechanics.

questions.question: A net force of 18 N acts on a 3 kg box. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
questions.explanation: Rearrange F = m·a to get a = F / m = 18 / 3 = 6 m/s². Multiplying instead (18 × 3 = 54) is the usual mistake: a bigger mass should give a smaller acceleration, not a bigger one.

questions.question: A heavy truck and a small car collide head-on. How do the forces they exert on each other compare?
choices: The truck pushes harder on the car
The car pushes harder on the truck
Only the truck exerts a force
The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction
questions.explanation: Newton's third law says the two forces in an interaction are always equal and opposite, whatever the masses. The car suffers more because the same force gives its smaller mass a much larger acceleration (a = F / m), not because it receives a bigger force.

questions.question: State Newton's first law in your own words, and say what it means for an object that is already moving.
questions.answer: An object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity, unless a net force acts on it. A moving object needs no force to keep going; a force is needed only to change its speed or direction.
questions.explanation: Everyday objects slow down because friction and air resistance act against their motion as a net force. Remove those forces, as in deep space, and an object keeps moving indefinitely.

questions.question: In a vacuum chamber, a 1 kg ball and a 10 kg ball are released from the same height at the same moment. What happens?
choices: The 10 kg ball lands first
They land at the same time
The 1 kg ball lands first
The 10 kg ball lands ten times sooner
questions.explanation: The 10 kg ball feels ten times the gravitational force, but it also has ten times the inertia, so both accelerate at g ≈ 9.8 m/s². Heavier objects only seem to fall faster in air when air resistance matters, as with a feather or a sheet of paper.
questions.concept: free fall does not depend on mass

questions.question: What is the weight, in newtons, of a 50 kg person on Earth? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
questions.explanation: Weight is W = m·g = 50 × 9.8 = 490 N. The 50 kg is the person's mass, which would be the same on the Moon; the weight in newtons is the force of gravity on that mass.

questions.question: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path, what is its acceleration?
choices: Zero, because it is momentarily at rest
9.8 m/s² upward
9.8 m/s² downward
It depends on how hard it was thrown
questions.explanation: Gravity never switches off, so the acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward for the whole flight, including the top. The velocity is zero at that instant, but zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration: the velocity is changing from upward to downward.
questions.concept: acceleration at the top of a throw

questions.question: You push sideways on a heavy box with a force of 100 N, but it does not move. How large is the static friction force on the box?
choices: Zero, because the box is not sliding
More than 100 N, or the box would move
It depends only on the box's weight
Exactly 100 N, opposite to your push
questions.explanation: The box is not accelerating, so the net force on it is zero and static friction must exactly balance your push. Static friction adjusts to match the applied force, up to a maximum. The box's weight, through the normal force, sets only that maximum, not the friction acting right now.

questions.question: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s crashes into a stationary 1 kg cart, and they stick together. What is their speed just after the collision, in m/s?
questions.explanation: Momentum before is 3 × 4 + 1 × 0 = 12 kg·m/s. Afterwards the combined 4 kg must carry the same 12 kg·m/s, so v = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s. Kinetic energy is not conserved here: it drops from 24 J to 18 J, with the rest turning into heat and sound.

questions.question: Why does an airbag reduce injuries in a car crash?
choices: It makes the stop take longer, so the force on the person is smaller
It reduces the person's total change in momentum
It removes the person's kinetic energy instantly
It increases the person's mass
questions.explanation: The person's change in momentum is fixed by their mass and speed. Since force × time = change in momentum, stretching out the stopping time lowers the force. The airbag does not reduce the momentum change; it spreads it over more time.

questions.question: A car's speed triples. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.explanation: KE = ½·m·v², so kinetic energy grows with the square of the speed: 3² = 9. Tripling the speed gives nine times the energy, not three times, which is why a crash at 90 km/h is far worse than one at 30 km/h.

questions.question: A waiter carries a tray across a room at constant speed, holding it level. How much work does his upward holding force do on the tray?
choices: The tray's weight times the distance walked
Zero, because the force is at right angles to the motion
A negative amount, because he stops it falling
It depends on how fast he walks
questions.explanation: Work counts only the distance moved in the direction of the force. The holding force points up while the tray moves sideways, so that force does no work. This fits with energy: the tray's speed and height stay the same, so its energy does not change.
questions.concept: work needs motion along the force

questions.question: A motor lifts a 20 kg crate 3 m straight up in 6 s at a steady speed. What is its power output, in watts? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
questions.explanation: The work done equals the potential energy gained: m·g·h = 20 × 9.8 × 3 = 588 J. Power is work per unit time: 588 / 6 = 98 W. Forgetting to divide by the time gives the energy (588 J), not the power.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of energy, and say what happens to a sliding box's kinetic energy as friction slows it down.
questions.answer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or changed from one form to another. As friction slows the box, its kinetic energy becomes thermal energy (heat) in the box and the floor, plus a little sound.
questions.explanation: Friction does not destroy energy; it moves it into forms that are hard to get back. The total energy of the box and its surroundings stays the same.

questions.question: Match each quantity to its SI unit.
questions.explanation: A newton is 1 kg·m/s², a joule is 1 N·m, and a watt is 1 J/s. Momentum, mass times velocity, has no special name, just kg·m/s.

questions.question: A cyclist rides at a constant 6 m/s for 10 s. What is the area under her velocity-time graph for that time, in meters?
questions.explanation: The graph is a flat line at 6 m/s, so the area is a rectangle: 6 × 10 = 60. The area under a velocity-time graph is the displacement, 60 m.

questions.question: On a position-time graph, an object's line is flat (horizontal) from t = 2 s to t = 5 s. What is the object doing then?
choices: Moving at a constant velocity
Standing still
Accelerating steadily
Moving back toward the start
questions.explanation: The slope of a position-time graph is the velocity. A flat line has zero slope: the position is not changing, so the object is at rest. On a velocity-time graph a flat line would instead mean constant velocity, which is the usual mix-up.

questions.question: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 6 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping, in meters?
questions.explanation: Use v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, u = 30 and a = −6: 0 = 900 − 12s, so s = 75 m. Using s = u·t without the acceleration term overestimates the distance.

questions.question: A ball rolls off a table at 3 m/s at the same moment an identical ball is dropped from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which hits the floor first?
choices: The rolling ball, because it is moving faster
The dropped ball, because its path is shorter
They land at the same time
It depends on how heavy the balls are
questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall the same height with the same g, so they land together; the rolling ball just lands farther away. The longer curved path does not slow its vertical fall.

questions.question: Put the steps for solving a force problem in order.
items: Isolate the object you are analyzing
Draw an arrow for every force acting on it
Add the forces to find the net force
Apply F = m·a to find the acceleration
questions.explanation: A free-body diagram comes first, so no force is forgotten and none from other objects sneaks in. Only after choosing a sign convention can you add forces correctly, and only the net force goes into F = m·a.

questions.question: Select every statement that is correct.
choices: An object moving at constant velocity has zero net force on it
A thrown ball has zero acceleration at the top of its flight
The two forces in a third law pair act on different objects
In a vacuum, a heavier object falls faster than a lighter one
A car turning a corner at constant speed is accelerating
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no net force (first law), third law pairs act on different objects, and changing direction is acceleration. At the top of a throw the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still g downward, and in a vacuum all masses fall with the same acceleration.

questions.question: A 50 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². How hard does the scale push up on her, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
questions.explanation: Taking up as positive: N − m·g = m·a, so N = m(g + a) = 50 × 11.8 = 590 N. Her weight is only 490 N; the extra 100 N is the net force that accelerates her upward.

questions.question: What is the momentum of a 1,200 kg car moving at 15 m/s, in kg·m/s?
questions.explanation: p = m·v = 1,200 × 15 = 18,000 kg·m/s, in the direction the car is moving.

questions.question: How much gravitational potential energy does a 4 kg box gain when it is lifted 2 m? Use g = 9.8 m/s² and answer in joules.
questions.explanation: PE = m·g·h = 4 × 9.8 × 2 = 78.4 J. Leaving out g gives 8, which is not an energy at all.

questions.question: A sled starts from rest at the top of a frictionless hill 20 m high. How fast is it moving at the bottom? Use g = 9.8 m/s².
choices: 14 m/s
28 m/s
questions.explanation: Potential energy becomes kinetic energy: m·g·h = ½·m·v², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 20) = √392 ≈ 19.8 m/s. The mass cancels, and so does the hill's shape. 392 m/s forgets the square root, and 14 m/s forgets the 2.

questions.question: A velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping downward that crosses the time axis at t = 4 s and continues below it. What happens at t = 4 s?
choices: The object is back at its starting point
The object's acceleration becomes zero
The object stops for an instant, then moves the opposite way
The object hits the ground
questions.explanation: Crossing the time axis means the velocity passes through zero and changes sign: a momentary stop followed by motion in the other direction. The slope, the acceleration, stays the same throughout. Returning to the start would need the areas above and below the axis to cancel.
